summary.text: Take \(n=8=2^3\), so \(\Omega(8)=3\) is odd and at least \(3\). Since the Möbius values on \(4\) and \(8\) vanish, the defining sum gives \(a(8)=8!(H_8-H_4)=25584>0\), contradicting the predicted negativity.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
H_m=\sum_{j=1}^m\frac1j
\]
be the \(m\)-th harmonic number, and let \(\mu\) denote the Möbius function. The sequence in the conjecture is given by the factorial-scaled Möbius transform
\[
a(n)=n!\sum_{d\mid n}\mu\!\left(\frac nd\right)H_d
\qquad(n\ge 1).
\]
We disprove the proposed sign characterization by taking \(n=8\).

First consider the right-hand side of the proposed equivalence. Since
\[
8=2^3=2\cdot2\cdot2,
\]
the total number of prime factors of \(8\), counted with multiplicity, is
\[
\Omega(8)=3.
\]
Thus \(\Omega(8)\) is odd and is at least \(3\). Consequently, the condition on the right-hand side of the conjectured equivalence is true for \(n=8\).

It remains to calculate the sign of \(a(8)\). The positive divisors of \(8\) are
\[
1,2,4,8.
\]
Accordingly, the Möbius-transform sum is
\[
\sum_{d\mid8}\mu\!\left(\frac8d\right)H_d
 =\mu(8)H_1+\mu(4)H_2+\mu(2)H_4+\mu(1)H_8.
\]
Recall that \(\mu(1)=1\), that \(\mu(p)=-1\) for a prime \(p\), and that \(\mu(m)=0\) whenever \(m\) is divisible by the square of a prime. Therefore
\[
\mu(1)=1,\qquad \mu(2)=-1,\qquad \mu(4)=0,\qquad \mu(8)=0.
\]
Indeed, both \(4=2^2\) and \(8=2^3\) are divisible by \(2^2\). Substitution into the divisor sum gives
\[
\sum_{d\mid8}\mu\!\left(\frac8d\right)H_d
=0\cdot H_1+0\cdot H_2-H_4+H_8
=H_8-H_4.
\]
The difference has a particularly simple form:
\[
H_8-H_4=\frac15+\frac16+\frac17+\frac18.
\]
Using the common denominator \(840\), this is
\[
\frac{168}{840}+\frac{140}{840}+\frac{120}{840}+\frac{105}{840}
=\frac{533}{840}.
\]
Equivalently, one may compute \(H_4=25/12\) and \(H_8=761/280\), whose difference is again \(533/840\). In particular, the Möbius-transform sum is strictly positive.

Since \(8!=40320\), it follows that
\[
a(8)=8!\,(H_8-H_4)
=40320\cdot\frac{533}{840}
=48\cdot533
=25584>0.
\]
Thus the assertion \(a(8)<0\) is false, whereas the assertion that \(\Omega(8)\) is odd and at least \(3\) is true. Hence, at the positive integer \(n=8\), the two sides of the proposed equivalence have different truth values. Therefore it is not true that for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
a(n)<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Omega(n)\text{ is odd and }\Omega(n)\ge3.
\]
This single counterexample disproves the conjecture.
